unmatched.line: Go to a place that calls your attention or evokes any personal memory in Waterloo. Using a field recorder, record sounds that characterize that place. You may record the sounds as you walk about that site if it feels appropriate. Later, in a quiet space (ideally a recording studio), record a personal narrative sharing your memory evoked by the site or the emotions or reasons for being there. Speak in the first person singular and the present tense. For instance: "I am standing next to the first building where I slept when I first landed in Canada." Or, "This is the walk-in clinic where a doctor saw me when I had terrible abdominal pain and did not have a family doctor." You may write your narrative first, rehearse it and then say it loud and record it. Use some of the recorded sounds and your voice as ingredients to compose a 2-3 minute digital audio project using Audacity or the DAW of your choice. Although I will not assess your skills as a storyteller, a clear story will be a bonus. To grade your work, I am looking at the quality of your recordings, the relationship between the sounds, the place and the story, and how you mixed and edited them to engage your audience. Submit a short written statement (1-2 pages, doubled space, font Times Roman size 12) reflecting on your experience of recording and editing the material. Submit both files -as a sound file and a word document- through peerScholar by Monday October 7, at noon.

Create a "soundtrack" for a short film clip (2 - 3 minutes long) of your choice. Most of the sounds in your soundtrack should be recorded by you. Do not use ready-made music or sound effects. You may use 'foley' sound, experimental sound, or a mix of both. You are not expected to add the sound to the video using video editing software. Submit the audio file along with a Word document in which you give a link to the short video clip (if possible) and a short statement (1-2 pages, doubled space, font Times Roman size 12) of what you intend to achieve by adding your sound to the clip. Submit both files -as a sound file and a word document- through peerScholar by Monday November 6, at noon.

unmatched.line: Research communication is a crucial skill. While the final thesis is the key vehicle for sharing research findings, due to its length and style, it won’t be readily accessible to the larger community. Accordingly, this assignment features the presentation of the thesis problem context, methods and key findings in the form of a poster to be presented and discussed in a group venue, likely the Atrium of EV1 or in the SERS Salon area in early April 2025. The Poster must be submitted via Dropbox by no later than 23:59 Thursday March 27 th . The Instructor will arrange to have them printed and distributed back to the students. The Instructor will convene a “poster session” in early April during which the Instructor, with assistance from several colleagues, will review the posters and discuss them with students. The Instructor will then assign final grades for the poster .

The main deliverable outcome of this course is the Senior Honours Thesis. Typically a Senior Honours Thesis is a long-form written document prepared to professional standards. The length and format vary by student and topic. It is strongly recommended that the thesis feature distinct sections as follows: Introduction, Literature Review, Methods, Results, Discussion, Conclusion. This approach will be discussed in class. It is not uncommon for a thesis in this form to be 20,000 words in length, inclusive of references and appendixes. That said, each student will negotiate the length and required content with their Supervisor with input from the Instructor as needed. The Final Thesis is due via Dropbox by 23:59 Friday April 7, 2025. The Thesis will be graded by the Supervisor.
